title: Osteogenesis Imperfecta: Type 1 Collagen Mutations, Sillence Types and Bisphosphonates
subject: ss-paediatric-endocrinology
module: Rickets, Calcium Disorders and Posterior Pituitary

steps.say: The vast majority of osteogenesis imperfecta cases stem from mutations in type one collagen alpha chains.
steps.tx: Characterize the classical genetics involving **COL1A1 and COL1A2 dominant genetics** in osteogenesis imperfecta. Over 85-90% of osteogenesis imperfecta is autosomal dominant, caused by mutations in COL1A1 (17q21.33) or COL1A2 (7q21.3) encoding the pro-alpha-1 and pro-alpha-2 chains of type 1 collagen; qualitative glycine substitutions cause severe structural deformity, whereas quantitative null mutations cause milder phenotypes.

vis.title: Type 1 Collagen Genetics in Osteogenesis Imperfecta
rows: Null alleles cause mild OI Type I; glycine substitutions cause severe Type II-IV
Point mutations disrupt triple helix folding and stability

steps.say: The Sillence classification stratifies osteogenesis imperfecta into four main clinical subtypes based on severity.
steps.tx: Classify clinical phenotypes using the **Sillence clinical classification (Types I-IV)** in pediatric practice. Classified into: Type I (mild, non-deforming, blue sclerae, quantitative defect), Type II (perinatal lethal, crumpling long bones, beaded ribs), Type III (progressively deforming, severe short stature), and Type IV (moderate deforming, normal sclerae).

vis.title: Sillence Classification of Osteogenesis Imperfecta
rows: Blue sclerae, childhood fractures, adult hearing loss, normal stature
Extreme bone fragility, crumpled femora, beaded ribs, lethal pulmonary hypoplasia
Severe bone deformity, extreme short stature, triangular facies, scoliosis
Normal sclerae, recurrent fractures, variable dentinogenesis imperfecta

steps.say: Extreme scleral thinning permits underlying choroidal pigment to show through as distinct blue sclerae.
steps.tx: Analyze the anatomical basis and diagnostic significance of the **Blue sclerae mechanism** in osteogenesis imperfecta. Blue sclerae result from extreme thinning of scleral collagen fibers, permitting the underlying dark pigmented choroid coat to become visually translucent; while classic in OI Type I, faint blue sclerae can be normal in neonates under 6 months due to physiological scleral thinness.

vis.alt: Composite medical illustration of osteogenesis imperfecta showing scleral thinning with blue hue, dentinogenesis imperfecta, and multiple bone fractures with intramedullary rodding.
vis.caption: Clinical and radiographic hallmarks of severe osteogenesis imperfecta.

steps.say: Dentinogenesis imperfecta manifests with discolored, translucent teeth that undergo accelerated attrition.
steps.tx: Recognize the dental and radiographic characteristics of **Dentinogenesis imperfecta hallmark** in osteogenesis imperfecta. Dentinogenesis imperfecta manifests with opalescent, amber or blue-gray teeth with accelerated attrition and pulp canal obliteration on dental panoramic radiography; defective type 1 collagen in dentin causes early enamel spalling and rapid dental destruction requiring early prosthodontic crowns.

vis.title: Dentinogenesis Imperfecta Diagnostic Characteristics
rows: Amber, translucent, yellow-brown or opalescent gray
Abnormal light diffraction through defective dentin
Abnormal dentinoenamel junction leading to enamel loss
Bulbous crowns, cervical constriction, obliteration of pulp canals
Rapid progressive dentin deposition filling pulp chamber

steps.say: Multiple accessory sutural ossicles known as Wormian bones appear classically along the lambdoid suture.
steps.tx: Identify the diagnostic significance of **Wormian bones on skull radiographs** in suspected osteogenesis imperfecta. Skull radiographs classically demonstrate >= 10 Wormian bones (mosaic islands of accessory suture ossification > 6 x 4 mm) along the lambdoid suture, serving as an essential skeletal marker to distinguish osteogenesis imperfecta and genetic fragility from non-accidental trauma.

vis.title: Radiological Differentiation in Suspected Bone Fragility

steps.say: Cyclical intravenous pamidronate reshapes compressed vertebral bodies and significantly reduces childhood fractures.
steps.tx: Administer cyclical bisphosphonate protocols following the **Intravenous pamidronate cyclical protocol** developed in Montreal. Cyclical intravenous pamidronate (1.0 mg/kg/day for 3 consecutive days every 3-4 months, cumulative annual dose 9 mg/kg/year) increases lumbar spine BMD Z-scores, reduces fracture rates, and reshapes collapsed vertebrae in growing children with moderate-to-severe osteogenesis imperfecta.

vis.alt: Cellular diagram of bone remodeling illustrating osteoblast-osteoclast coupling, RANK ligand pathway, and osteoclast inhibition by bisphosphonate therapy.
vis.caption: Targeted inhibition of osteoclast-mediated bone resorption by cyclical bisphosphonates.

steps.say: Intravenous zoledronic acid offers a convenient single-day infusion alternative with equivalent therapeutic efficacy.
steps.tx: Utilize outpatient bisphosphonate regimens incorporating **Intravenous zoledronic acid infusion** for pediatric OI management. Intravenous zoledronic acid (0.05 mg/kg IV infused over 30-45 minutes every 6 months) provides equivalent bone remineralization with fewer hospital visits compared to multi-day pamidronate; patients require pre-infusion hydration and verification of normal serum calcium and vitamin D.

left.title: Cyclical Pamidronate
points: Longest safety record and proven vertebral reshaping
Requires multi-day hospital or day-care admission

right.title: Zoledronic Acid
points: Single 30-45 minute infusion once every 6 months
Greater convenience and reduced healthcare burden

steps.say: Severe cranial base deformities in osteogenesis imperfecta risk life-threatening brainstem compression.
steps.tx: Conduct systematic neurological and radiological **Basilar invagination neurological surveillance** in severely affected children. Severe OI types III and IV are complicated by platybasia and basilar invagination (odontoid protrusion into foramen magnum), requiring cervical spine CT/MRI screening for brainstem compression, progressive myelopathy, lower cranial nerve palsies, or central sleep apnea.
